messages.content: How far will a car travel in time 't' when launched with velocity 'v' at an angle 'theta'?

function.name: calculate_projectile_range
function.description: Calculate the range of a projectile launched at an angle with initial velocity, using the kinematic equation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

initial_velocity.description: The initial velocity at which projectile is launched. This is a float type value.

angle.description: The angle at which projectile is launched. This should be in degrees. This is a float type value.

time.description: The time in seconds after which the range is to be calculated. This is a float type value.

message.content:
**Horizontal distance travelled**

If the “car” behaves like a point mass projected from ground level without friction or drag, its horizontal motion is uniform:

\[
x(t)\;=\;\underbrace{v\,\cos \theta}_{\text{constant horizontal speed}}\times t .
\]

So the distance covered along the ground during a time interval \(t\) is simply  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle D_{\text{ground}}(t)=v\,\cos(\theta)\;t } 
\]

*Units:*  
– \(D_{\text{ground}}\) in metres (if \(v\) is m/s and \(t\) in s),  
– \(v\) in m/s,  
– \(\theta\) in radians (or convert deg → rad).

---

### What about the actual trajectory?

While the horizontal component stays constant, the vertical coordinate follows

\[
y(t)=v\,\sin\theta\,t-\frac12gt^{2},
\]
with \(g\simeq9.81~\mathrm{m/s^{2}}\).

If you’re interested in **the true path length** up to time \(t\),

\[
s(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\sqrt{[v\cos\theta]^{2}
+\bigl[v\sin\theta-gt\bigr]^{2}}\;dt ,
\]

which has no elementary closed‑form solution but can be evaluated numerically.

---

#### Quick sanity check

| \(v\) | \(\theta\) | \(t\) | Horizontal distance |
|-------|------------|------|---------------------|
| 20 m/s | 30° | 5 s | \(20\times\cos30^\circ\times5≈17.32×5≈86.6\) m |

Feel free to plug your own numbers into the first formula!
